module.title: Inference, serving and model operations
module.summary: Score a table and answer a request from the same registered version, hold the endpoint to a contract, size its concurrency, release and roll back by traffic, and read drift as a hypothesis that delayed labels test.
objectives: Choose batch or online scoring for a consumer and trace one online request across its identities, contract check, feature lookup and timing.
Write a local contract test, size provisioned concurrency from arrival rate and service time, and plan a staged release with a one-step rollback.

Read inference tables and a data profiling monitor as evidence, separate drift from verified quality loss under delayed labels, classify an incident and fill an operational scorecard without provisioning anything.

scenarios.title: Write the release, rollback and monitoring runbook for the defect-risk endpoint
scenarios.context: Fictional Cinderline Components serves its coating defect-risk model two ways: a nightly batch job scores every part produced that day into a Delta table the inspection planner reads, and an end-of-line station calls a Model Serving endpoint named defect-risk and diverts a part to the inspection lane when the returned risk is 0.35 or higher, within a 200 ms budget. Version 7 serves under the alias champion; version 8 was trained on three more months of data and scores 0.03 better on held-out precision. Inspection labels arrive one to three days later for diverted parts and for a random 5% audit sample; other parts get a label only from a customer return, weeks later or never. Two features are looked up from an online store at request time. The plant runs two shifts; the humid season starts next month. No endpoint, monitor or job is created in this task, and cost figures are unknown until current pricing is checked.
scenarios.task: Write a one-page runbook for the operations lead: the staged release of version 8 with the evidence gate at each stage and the one-step rollback, the operational scorecard with each measurement's source and owner, the contract test that must pass before any version is served, and the incident classification the on-call engineer follows. Mark what is known, what is hypothesized and what cannot be measured until labels arrive.
requirements: Stage the release as a traffic split with an evidence gate per stage, and state the rollback as a single configuration change that keeps the old served entity available.
Separate endpoint health, contract, data and feature, and verified model quality as four incident classes, each with its own first check and mitigation.
Give every scorecard row a source (endpoint metrics, inference table, monitor, labels or billing), an owner and a target, and label drift rows as hypotheses until labels test them.
State the delayed-label limits honestly: which rows will have labels, when, and which quality numbers therefore cannot be verified for unflagged parts without the audit sample.
scenarios.model:
### Release and rollback
Stage 0: version 8's signature passes the local contract test (the column list, a valid dataframe_split body, and the missing-column, renamed-column and unit-suffix cases, sent as JSON through open-source MLflow's request handler) and a batch replay over last week's inference-table rows, compared with version 7's logged responses. Stage 1: add version 8 as a second served entity at 10% traffic for two days; gate on error rate, P99 latency inside the 200 ms budget and a flagged rate within the 6 to 12% band, all read per served entity from the inference table. Stage 2: 50% for three days; gate adds precision on diverted parts once the first labels arrive, compared with version 7 over the same windows. Stage 3: 100%, version 7 kept as a served entity for seven days. Rollback at any stage: one configuration update setting version 7 to 100%; version 8 stays deployed at 0% for diagnosis. Never roll back by deleting the endpoint.

### Scorecard
Availability and P99 latency from endpoint health metrics (platform owner, targets 99.5% and 120 ms); 4xx and 5xx rates from the exported endpoint metrics, explained by inference-table status codes and bodies that can arrive up to an hour later (station app owner for 4xx, platform for 5xx, target under 0.1%); feature freshness as publish lag, the time since the online store's latest publish (feature pipeline owner, under 60 minutes); flagged rate and input drift from the data profiling monitor (model owner; the 6 to 12% band is a trigger, not a verdict); label coverage from the inspection join (quality owner; all diverted parts plus the 5% audit); verified precision on diverted parts from inspection labels with their lag, and audit-sample recall over a trailing week with its count of defective parts; daily cost from billing once pricing is checked.

### Contract test
Read the version's signature from its MLmodel file, wrap it around a constant stand-in model, and send JSON bodies through open-source MLflow's request handler: the signature names the seven station columns, a valid dataframe_split body is accepted, and bodies missing coat_thickness_um, naming it thickness_um, or sending humidity_pct as "61%" are refused with 400. The test proves the contract, not the model's predictions; it runs locally, calls no managed endpoint, and whether the managed endpoint parses exactly as the open-source server does is checked at stage 1 through the 4xx rate.

### Incident classes
Endpoint health (5xx, timeouts, latency without a request change): roll traffic back if a release is in progress, then read service logs and capacity. Contract (4xx spike): find the caller change, fix the caller or map the field, never widen the signature under incident. Data and features (nulls, freshness, drift): stop the rollout, fix the pipeline, backfill, return an explicit no-score for a missing lookup instead of an imputed zero, and treat any quality claim as hypothesis. Verified quality loss (labelled windows worse than baseline): roll back to version 7 if the loss followed a release, fix the pipeline and backfill if a data incident preceded it, and retrain only when labels show the world changed. Every incident records what was known at each time, and the humid season is pre-declared as an expected input shift so a drift alert alone does not open a quality incident.
scenarios.reasoning: The runbook makes release and rollback the same lever, ties each scorecard row to the system that can actually measure it, keeps the contract test local and honest about what it does not prove, and refuses to let drift stand in for verified loss when labels are delayed and biased toward diverted parts.

rubric.criterion: Staged release with a reversible rollback
rubric.weak: Deploy version 8 and watch; rollback described as redeploying version 7.
rubric.partial: Traffic percentages named but no evidence gate per stage, or the old entity removed before the gate.
rubric.strong: Each stage has a measurable gate read per served entity; rollback is one traffic change with the old entity retained and the new one kept for diagnosis.

rubric.weak: All alerts lead to retraining or to a rollback.
rubric.partial: Health and quality separated but a 4xx spike or a null feature attributed to the model.
rubric.strong: Four classes with a first check and a mitigation each; a caller's schema change and a feature-pipeline failure are named as non-model incidents.

rubric.weak: A list of metrics with no source or owner.
rubric.partial: Sources named but drift rows presented as quality verdicts, or cost given as a number without a pricing source.
rubric.strong: Every row has source, owner, target and a known or hypothesized status; cost is marked unknown until pricing is checked.

rubric.weak: Precision and recall reported as if labels were complete.
rubric.partial: Label lag acknowledged but selection bias toward diverted parts ignored.
rubric.strong: States which rows get labels and when, uses the audit sample for unflagged parts, and reports verified numbers with their lag.

disclosures.question: Can the station tolerate a cold start if we enable scale to zero to save money overnight?
disclosures.response: No. The first request after a scale-down waits seconds to minutes with no promised time, and a part that waits past 200 ms passes uninspected. Scale to zero is refused for this endpoint; the cost is accepted and marked unknown until pricing is checked.

disclosures.question: Will the humid season make the model wrong?
disclosures.response: Unknown. It will move the humidity input and probably the flagged rate. Whether precision on diverted parts changes is only knowable when labels arrive, so the season is recorded as an expected input shift and the quality question stays open until then.

disclosures.question: Do we have labels for parts that were not diverted?
disclosures.response: Only for the 5% audit sample and for customer returns. Recall on unflagged parts is estimated from the audit sample alone and reported with its sample size.

claims.description: Model Serving deploys MLflow models as REST endpoints without managed infrastructure on the customer's side and supports real-time and batch inference for custom models.

A registered model can score a Spark DataFrame through mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf, loaded by name and alias from Unity Catalog; AI Functions such as ai_query can call served models from SQL, including traditional ML models deployed on Model Serving endpoints.
claims.context: Batch inference on Databricks; ai_query support is checked per model type.

claims.description: A model logged with the feature engineering client keeps references to its features, and FeatureEngineeringClient.score_batch joins point-in-time correct feature values from the offline store to rows that carry only the keys before scoring.
claims.context: Feature Engineering in Unity Catalog; batch path.

claims.description: Open-source MLflow's scoring server accepts exactly one of the four input keys, parses the JSON body with the signature's types before prediction, then enforces the signature, so a castable value is accepted and an uncastable one is refused as a bad request.
claims.context: Open-source MLflow 3.x; the managed endpoint is verified separately.

claims.description: An endpoint holds served entities with a workload size mapped to a provisioned-concurrency range (Small 4, Medium 8 to 16, Large 16 to 64 as read at search time), one unit of concurrency serves one request at a time, required concurrency is estimated as queries per second times model execution time, and scale to zero lets the lower bound reach zero after 30 minutes of inactivity, followed by a cold start of usually ten to twenty seconds and sometimes minutes with no SLA.
Requests carry a JSON-serialized pandas DataFrame under dataframe_split or dataframe_records, or tensors under instances or inputs, and the response returns predictions.
One endpoint can serve several models or versions with a configured traffic percentage per served entity, so a release and a rollback are traffic changes.
claims.context: Traffic split on custom model endpoints.

claims.description: Inference tables log each request and response as rows of a Delta table in Unity Catalog, which can be joined with labels to evaluate and retrain.
claims.context: Inference tables; prerequisites are listed on the applicable variant's page.

claims.description: Data profiling (formerly Lakehouse Monitoring) computes profile and drift metric tables for a monitored table; the InferenceLog profile adds model performance metrics when prediction and label columns are provided and drift when a baseline table or consecutive windows exist.

MLflow schema enforcement validates inputs against the model signature before the model runs: missing required inputs raise, undeclared inputs are ignored, and only lossless type conversions are accepted for column-based signatures, such as int to double but not long to double.
For a model logged with the feature engineering client, the serving endpoint uses the entity keys in a request to look up precomputed features from an online store at inference time.

Endpoint health metrics report latency, request rate, error rate, CPU and memory and can be exported to Prometheus and Datadog; service and build logs support deployment debugging; data profiling covers model performance and drift.

concepts.definition: Scoring a whole table with a loaded model version and writing the predictions back as columns with their provenance.
A managed REST endpoint that routes each request to a served model version and returns a JSON prediction.
The exact JSON shape, column names and types an endpoint accepts and the response it returns, fixed by the model signature.
The number of requests an endpoint can process at the same time; requests beyond it wait, and a sustained excess grows a backlog.
Precomputed features fetched from an online store by the keys in a request instead of being sent by the caller.
The percentage of requests an endpoint routes to each served entity, changed by a configuration update.
A Delta table in which the endpoint logs each request, its response, status, served entity and timing.
A measured change in the distribution of inputs or predictions between windows or against a baseline, which does not by itself prove quality loss.
The true outcome that arrives after the prediction, only for some rows, and only then permits a verified quality measurement.
A table of named measurements for a served model, each with its source, owner, target and whether it is known or hypothesized.
